strengths: The paper addresses a useful retrieval setting: combining a reference person image with descriptions of appearance changes. SynCPR’s 1.15 million synthetic triplets and ITCPR’s 2,202 real-image queries could provide valuable resources for this research community.

Generating paired images within a single canvas is a practical insight for improving identity consistency. The synthesis pipeline combines diverse textual prompts, domain adaptation, and multimodal filtering in a coherent design.

The reported improvements are meaningful. With both methods trained on SynCPR, FAFA exceeds SPRC by 4.27 percentage points in Rank-1 and 3.98 points in mAP. Table S3 also reports improvements on CIRR, providing evidence beyond the newly introduced benchmark.

The presentation is generally clear, with informative diagrams and substantial supplementary detail. Component ablations, filtering experiments, and dataset-size studies provide useful evidence, while the appendices document prompts and many training settings.
weaknesses: The principal concern is test-set-driven model selection. Appendix B.1.3 explicitly reserves ITCPR for testing, but Section 4.3 and Appendix C.4 select the filtering threshold, alpha, k, auxiliary-loss weights, and masking ratio using performance on this benchmark. No separate validation protocol or untouched CPR test set is reported. This undermines the independence of the headline evaluation and is the main reason for the rejection recommendation.

The central claims of high-quality, identity-consistent, and demographically comprehensive synthetic data are insufficiently validated. There is no independent human audit reporting identity errors, caption correctness, or agreement with the MLLM evaluator. Averaging four scores can also admit weak identity consistency when other scores are high. Qualitative examples and downstream retrieval gains do not establish these stronger dataset claims.

The evaluation does not fully establish the claimed use of complementary modalities. Although retraining CaLa and SPRC on SynCPR is valuable, image-only, text-only, and simple fusion controls are not comparably trained on SynCPR with the same backbone. Such controls would separate compositional reasoning from domain adaptation. No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported; the additional MFR gain over FDA plus FD is only 0.49 Rank-1 points and 0.11 mAP points.

ITCPR annotation reliability needs stronger documentation. Appendix B.1.2 uses candidates retrieved by a visual encoder to discover missing positives, but does not specify the candidate depth, annotator agreement, or an independent completeness audit. This procedure is helpful but does not substantiate the assertion that false negatives have been eliminated.

Important implementation details remain unspecified despite the extensive appendix: the number of query tokens, feature dimension, reconstruction-decoder architecture, and ID/GID batch sampling. Sampling is particularly consequential because the proposed soft labels require related examples to co-occur in a batch. The methodological positioning also needs sharpening: top-k query-token matching is a modest extension of BLIP-2’s existing query-based matching, and the relationship to prior synthetic CIR pipelines receives limited analysis.

The research-ethics discussion is insufficient for a system intended to identify people across clothing changes. The paper does not document applicable reuse and redistribution permissions for the real-person datasets or discuss non-consensual tracking and demographic performance disparities. Synthetic training images reduce additional collection, but fine-tuning on real-person images does not by itself establish privacy protection.
